newsitem.title: USA: USDA sets 2.3 Mln tonne FY97 sugar import quota.
newsitem.headline: USDA sets 2.3 Mln tonne FY97 sugar import quota.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department said Friday it set the fiscal 1997 sugar import quota at 2.3 million tonnes, or 2,535,316 short tons, with 1.7 million tonnes, or 1.873,929 short tons, to be allocated among importing nations immediately and the rest hinging on reviews set for January, March and May.
The U.S. Trade Representative's office was expected to announce the initial country by country allocations on Monday.
Under the formula adopted by USDA, an additional 200,000 tonnes of sugar would be allocated on each review date if the projected stocks to use ratio is below 15.5 percent.
If the stocks ratio is above 15.5 percent, the 200,000 tonne increase would be canceled.
USDA said it reserved the power to increase the tariff-rate quota at any time, if conditions warrant.

The Philippines, Brazil and Dominican Republic will be issued quota certificates that allow them to ship up to 25 percent of their quota during each quarter of fiscal 1997. Unentered allocations can be carried into other quarters.
USDA split the quota for refined and specialty sugar into three parts but with a maximum refined sugar quota of 47,000 tonnes, or 51,809 short tons.

The three parts include a specialty sugar quota of 1,656 tonnes, a most-favored-nation quota of 20,344 tonnes, or 22,425 short tons, and an allocation to Mexico. The U.S. trade office will announce later how the MFN quota will be divided.
Mexico was given an allocation of 25,000 tonnes, or 27,588 short tons, which can be filled with either raw or refined sugar.
Steve Hammond, USDA team leader on the sugar quota, said the quota proposed by USDA would result in a 14.3 percent stocks to use ratio based on current data.
The USDA quota was set at a lower level than the 2.475 million tonnes that was proposed in August and the amount for initial allocation also was reduced.
USDA set the review dates for later times than originally proposed. Hammond said that would allow more precise data to be used in any adjustment of the import quota.
Brazil, the Philippines and the Dominican Republic are the largest quota holders among three or four dozen nations.
